title: Answering the Watch Tower's Verses
subtitle: The verses a Jehovah's Witness raises to deny that Jesus is God — each with the orthodox, debate-ready answer. The mirror image of the positive case in 'The Divinity of Christ.'
displayTranslationNote: Displayed English Scripture is the Douay-Rheims (DRA), matching the rest of the site, verified against drbo.org (Challoner). Where the Greek or Hebrew decides the dispute, the original language is given with transliteration. NWT renderings (New World Translation, 2013 revision) are quoted where the rendering itself is part of the dispute and were verified against jw.org / Watchtower Online Library.
methodologyNote: Each argument here is a Jehovah's Witness OBJECTION: the title states the verse as a Witness uses it, and the explanation gives the Catholic/orthodox answer. The recurring keys are (1) the two natures of Christ — true God and true man — so texts of subjection, prayer, ignorance, or 'my God' describe the Son as man or in his incarnate mission, not a deficiency in his divine nature; (2) economic/functional order is not inferiority of nature; (3) word studies (firstborn=heir, archE=source/ruler, echad=united one, 'greater'=rank); (4) the 'only true God' / monotheism verses are the Trinity's own premise, not a refutation of it. Contested or two-edged texts (Proverbs 8, Revelation 3:14 archE, John 14:28) are rated honestly and listed under 'Honest caveats.'

arguments.title: “The Father is greater than I” — John 14:28
arguments.shortClaim: The Witness argues that if the Father is 'greater' than Jesus, then Jesus cannot be God — he must be a lesser, created being.

primaryReferences.text: You have heard that I said to you: I go away, and I come unto you. If you loved me, you would indeed be glad, because I go to the Father: for the Father is greater than I.
Who being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and in habit found as a man.

originalLanguage.note: 'meizōn' (greater) is the comparative of 'megas' (great) — greater in rank, position, or glory. It is NOT 'kreittōn' (better/superior in nature/quality). Jesus speaks these words in his humbled, incarnate state and in the context of 'I go to the Father' — i.e., he is returning to the heavenly glory he had 'before the world was' (John 17:5). Compare Philippians 2:6, where the same Christ is 'equal' (isa) with God, a statement of nature. Greatness of position (the Father, as unoriginate source within the Godhead, and as the one to whom the incarnate Son is obedient) is fully compatible with equality of nature.

arguments.nwtRebuttal: The NWT reads: 'the Father is greater than I am.' The wording is not itself disputed — the verse is true on any reading. The dispute is only what 'greater' means. The Watch Tower takes it as greater in nature (so Jesus is a creature); the orthodox answer is greater in position/office, spoken by the Son in his humbled human state.
arguments.explanation: This verse is true, and Catholics affirm it. The question is what kind of 'greater.' Two facts settle it. First, Jesus speaks as the incarnate Son who has 'emptied himself' and taken 'the form of a servant' (Philippians 2:7); in that humbled state the Father in heavenly glory is indeed greater, which is exactly why Jesus says it in the same breath as 'I go to the Father.' Second, the same Paul who records the humbling also says Christ was 'equal with God' (Philippians 2:6, Greek 'isa'). Greater in office, equal in nature — a son can be fully as human as his father while still owing him obedience. 'Greater' answers a question of rank, not of being. Press the Witness: John 14:28 says 'greater,' not 'better than' and not 'other in nature'; and the very next chapter has Jesus claim the works, the glory, and the honour of God.

arguments.title: “The Son also himself shall be subject” — 1 Corinthians 15:28
arguments.shortClaim: The Witness argues that if the Son is finally 'subject' to the Father, he cannot be co-equal God.

primaryReferences.text: And when all things shall be subdued unto him, then the Son also himself shall be subject unto him that put all things under him, that God may be all in all.

originalLanguage.note: 'hypotassō' (to be subject/ordered under) describes functional, relational order, not a difference of nature. Scripture uses the same verb of the mutual subjection of equals (Ephesians 5:21, Christians 'subject one to another') and of Christ, as a child, subject to Mary and Joseph (Luke 2:51) — without implying he was less human than they. The subjection here is that of the incarnate Son in his mediatorial, messianic role, which is handed back to the Father when its purpose ('that God may be all in all') is complete.

arguments.explanation: Subjection is about order, not nature. A son can be entirely equal to his father in humanity and still be rightly subject to him; subjection between persons who share a nature is ordinary, not a demotion. Here Paul describes the end of Christ's mediatorial kingdom: having subdued every enemy (v. 25-26), the incarnate Son, as head of redeemed humanity, offers the completed kingdom back so that 'God may be all in all.' This is the Son's economic role in salvation, freely undertaken in the incarnation, not evidence that his divine nature is inferior. Note that the Son's subjection is voluntary and functional; the Arian reading has to smuggle 'inferior in being' into a word ('hypotassō') that nowhere carries it.

arguments.title: “My God and your God” — John 20:17
arguments.shortClaim: The Witness argues that if Jesus calls the Father 'my God,' then Jesus has a God over him and therefore is not God.

primaryReferences.text: Jesus saith to her: Do not touch me, for I am not yet ascended to my Father. But go to my brethren, and say to them: I ascend to my Father and to your Father, to my God and your God.
Thomas answered, and said to him: My Lord, and my God.

arguments.explanation: The incarnate Son, having become truly man, can rightly worship and address the Father as 'my God' according to his human nature — that is what it means for the Word to have taken 'the form of a servant.' This no more cancels his divinity than his hunger or his death does. The decisive detail is the one the Witness overlooks: Jesus says 'my Father and your Father, my God and your God' — he carefully does NOT say 'our Father' or 'our God,' because his sonship and his relation to the Father are of a different order than ours (he is Son by nature, we by adoption). And in the SAME chapter, only eleven verses later, Thomas addresses this same risen Jesus as 'my Lord and my God' (John 20:28) and Jesus accepts it. John frames the chapter so that the Son calls the Father 'my God' as man, and is himself called 'my God' as God — the two natures side by side.

arguments.title: “The head of Christ is God” — 1 Corinthians 11:3
arguments.shortClaim: The Witness argues that if God is the 'head' of Christ, Christ is subordinate and therefore not God.

primaryReferences.text: But I would have you know, that the head of every man is Christ; and the head of the woman is the man; and the head of Christ is God.

originalLanguage.note: 'kephalē' (head) denotes source or ordered headship, not superior nature. Paul's own chain disproves the Arian use: 'the head of the woman is the man' — yet man and woman share one and the same human nature (Genesis 2:23). By the same logic, the Father being 'head' of Christ names an order of relation, not an inequality of nature. The headship applies pre-eminently to the Son in his incarnate, mediatorial role.

arguments.explanation: Headship in Paul is about order and source, not rank of being. Read the whole verse: Paul says man is the 'head' of woman — but no one concludes a woman is a lesser kind of creature than a man; they are equally human (Genesis 2:23, 'bone of my bones'). So 'the head of Christ is God' names a relational order within equality, not a difference of nature. Applied to Christ, it fits his voluntary place as the incarnate Son and mediator who does the Father's will. The verse is rated 'strong' rather than decisive only because it requires the Witness to grant the man/woman parallel Paul himself draws; once granted, the Arian inference collapses.

arguments.title: “God hath made him both Lord and Christ” — Acts 2:36
arguments.shortClaim: The Witness argues that if God 'made' Jesus Lord, then Jesus was not Lord by nature — he was promoted, like a creature.

primaryReferences.text: Therefore let all the house of Israel know most certainly, that God hath made both Lord and Christ, this same Jesus, whom you have crucified.
For which cause God also hath exalted him, and hath given him a name which is above all names: That in the name of Jesus every knee should bow...

originalLanguage.text: καὶ κύριον αὐτὸν καὶ χριστὸν ἐποίησεν ὁ θεός
originalLanguage.translit: kai kyrion auton kai christon epoiēsen ho theos
originalLanguage.note: 'epoiēsen' (made) here means 'constituted/declared/appointed to an office,' not 'created out of nothing.' Peter is speaking of the resurrection-exaltation: the one the Jews crucified has been publicly installed as Messiah ('Christ') and enthroned as 'Lord' (Kyrios, the LXX word for YHWH). It names a new public status given to the risen incarnate Son in his humanity, not the origin of his being.

arguments.explanation: 'Made' here is 'appointed/declared,' not 'created.' Peter's sermon is about the resurrection: the crucified Jesus has now been openly enthroned and vindicated as 'Lord and Christ.' That is a statement about his messianic office and his public exaltation as man, not about when he came to exist. The parallel is Philippians 2:9-11, where God 'exalts' the already-divine Son who had humbled himself. Note too that the title given is 'Lord' (Kyrios), the Greek Old Testament's own rendering of the divine name YHWH — so if anything the verse exalts Jesus into the divine name, it does not demote him. Rated 'strong' because the force depends on reading 'made' as 'appointed,' which the resurrection context clearly supports.

arguments.title: “The firstborn of every creature” — Colossians 1:15
arguments.shortClaim: The Witness argues that 'firstborn of all creation' means Jesus is the first and highest created being — part of creation, not the Creator.

primaryReferences.text: Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature:

For in him were all things created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, or dominations, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him and in him. And he is before all, and by him all things consist.

primaryReferences.citation: Psalm 89:27 (= Psalm 88:28 in the Douay-Rheims/Vulgate numbering)
primaryReferences.text: And I will make him my firstborn, high above the kings of the earth.

originalLanguage.note: 'prōtotokos' (firstborn) is a title of RANK, heirship, and pre-eminence, not of chronological creation. In Psalm 89:27 (LXX 88:28) God makes David 'firstborn' — David was the youngest son (1 Samuel 16:11-13); 'firstborn' there plainly means supreme heir. Had Paul meant 'first-created,' Greek had the word 'prōtoktistos' (first-created), which he does NOT use. The genitive 'of every creature / of all creation' is a genitive of subordination ('firstborn OVER all creation'), as v. 16 immediately explains: 'FOR in him all things were created.'

arguments.nwtRebuttal: The NWT reads 'the firstborn of all creation' at v. 15, then (at v. 16-17) inserts the word 'other' four times — 'by means of him all OTHER things were created' — so that Jesus becomes the first creature who then made the remaining 'other' things. The word 'other' is not in the Greek. The insertion is the device that turns 'firstborn' into 'first-created.' Remove it and v. 16 proves the opposite: he created all things, so he is not among created things.
arguments.explanation: 'Firstborn' in the Bible is a title of status, not a birth certificate. God calls David his 'firstborn' even though David was his father's youngest son (Psalm 89:27; 1 Samuel 16), and calls Israel his 'firstborn' nation (Exodus 4:22). It means supreme heir, pre-eminent one. Paul says exactly why Christ holds that rank over creation in the very next verse: 'FOR in him all things were created... all things were created by him and in him' (Colossians 1:16). The Creator of all things is not himself one of the created things. If Paul had wanted to say 'first created,' Greek has a precise word for that (prōtoktistos) and he avoided it. The whole Watch Tower reading hangs on the inserted word 'other' in v. 16, which has no basis in the Greek.

arguments.title: “The beginning of the creation of God” — Revelation 3:14
arguments.shortClaim: The Witness argues that if Jesus is 'the beginning of the creation of God,' he is the first thing God created.

primaryReferences.text: And to the angel of the church of Laodicea write: These things saith the Amen, the faithful and true witness, who is the beginning of the creation of God:
I am the First and the Last, And alive, and was dead, and behold I am living for ever and ever, and have the keys of death and of hell.

originalLanguage.text: ἡ ἀρχὴ τῆς κτίσεως τοῦ θεοῦ
originalLanguage.translit: hē archē tēs ktiseōs tou theou
originalLanguage.note: 'archē' means beginning, but also origin, source, and ruler (it is the root of 'archōn,' ruler, and 'archē,' principality/dominion). Read in the active sense — 'the Source/Originator/Ruler of God's creation' — it agrees with Revelation 1:17-18 (Jesus as First and Last) and Colossians 1:16 (all things created in him). The NWT's 'the beginning of the creation by God' presses the passive sense (Jesus as the first thing created). The word genuinely bears both senses; context and the rest of Revelation favour the active one.

arguments.nwtRebuttal: The NWT reads: 'the beginning of the creation by God,' understood as the first creature God made. The honest point in debate: 'archē' can be read passively ('beginning' = first created) or actively ('origin/ruler'); the Greek allows both, so this verse alone will not settle the argument. Lean on the clearer texts (Colossians 1:16, John 1:3) and use Revelation 3:14 as corroboration read in context.
arguments.explanation: The Greek word 'archē' is the same root English keeps in 'architect' (chief builder) and 'monarch' (sole ruler): it means not just a point in time but a source, origin, or ruler. Read that way, Jesus is 'the Source/Ruler of God's creation,' which matches how the same book has him say 'I am the First and the Last... who was dead and is alive' (Revelation 1:17-18) — a title of YHWH, not of a creature. Be honest with the Witness: this one verse is two-edged, because 'archē' can also mean a starting point. That is exactly why it should not be your lead argument. Settle the question with Colossians 1:16 and John 1:3 (he made all things that were made), then read Revelation 3:14 in their light.

arguments.title: “The Lord created/possessed me” — Proverbs 8:22-31 (Wisdom)
arguments.shortClaim: The Witness argues that Wisdom in Proverbs 8 (identified with the pre-incarnate Christ) says it was 'created' by God, proving Jesus is a creature.

primaryReferences.text: The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways, before he made any thing from the beginning.
I was with him forming all things: and was delighted every day, playing before him at all times.

originalLanguage.note: The Hebrew verb 'qanah' means to possess, acquire, or beget as readily as to create (e.g., Genesis 4:1, Eve 'qanah/gotten' a son; Genesis 14:19, God 'possessor' of heaven and earth). The DRA ('possessed me') follows this sense; the Septuagint chose 'ektise me' ('created me'), which is what the fourth-century Arians seized on. TWO cautions: (1) the lexical choice is genuinely contested, and (2) identifying the personified 'Wisdom' of this Hebrew poem with the pre-incarnate Son is an interpretive tradition, not a statement the New Testament makes directly.

arguments.nwtRebuttal: The NWT reads: 'Jehovah produced me as the beginning of his way,' leaning on the LXX 'created' sense. This is a weak proof-text for the Witness because it depends on BOTH a disputed translation of 'qanah' AND the assumption that this Hebrew poem's personified Wisdom is literally the Son speaking.
arguments.explanation: Be candid in debate: this is the Witness's weakest strong-sounding verse, and you should say so first — it earns credibility. Two problems undercut it. First, the Hebrew word (qanah) normally means 'possessed, acquired, brought forth,' not 'created from nothing'; the same word has Eve 'getting' a son and God as 'possessor' of heaven and earth (Genesis 4:1; 14:19). The DRA rightly reads 'possessed me.' Second, and more basic, Proverbs 8 is Hebrew wisdom poetry personifying God's attribute of Wisdom as a figure who speaks — the way Proverbs also personifies Folly as a woman. Reading that poetic figure as a literal autobiography of the pre-incarnate Son is a traditional application (the Fathers used it devotionally), not something the New Testament asserts. So do not stake the debate on Proverbs 8. If the Witness presses it, grant the ambiguity and return to the clear New Testament texts (John 1:1-3; Colossians 1:16; John 8:58).

arguments.title: “The Lord our God is one Lord” — Deuteronomy 6:4 / Mark 12:29 (the Shema)
arguments.shortClaim: The Witness argues that the Shema teaches God is one single person, so the Trinity (and a divine Christ) contradicts monotheism.

primaryReferences.text: Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord.
And Jesus answered him: The first commandment of all is, Hear, O Israel: the Lord thy God is one God.

originalLanguage.text: שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ יְהוָה אֶחָד
originalLanguage.translit: Shema Yisrael YHWH Eloheinu YHWH echad
originalLanguage.note: The operative word is 'echad' (one). 'echad' can denote a UNITED or compound oneness, not only a solitary unit: 'the two shall be one (echad) flesh' (Genesis 2:24); the spies carried 'one (echad) cluster' of grapes (Numbers 13:23). Hebrew has a different word for an absolute, solitary one — 'yachid' — which the Shema does NOT use. So the Shema asserts there is exactly one God (which the Trinity affirms) without defining that one God as unipersonal. CAUTION: 'echad' most often simply means the numeral one; use it to show the Shema does not EXCLUDE the Trinity, not to prove plurality from the word alone.

arguments.explanation: Catholics confess the Shema wholeheartedly: there is one and only one God. The Trinity is not three gods; it is the one God existing as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. So this verse is not an objection to the Catholic position — it is the Catholic position's own foundation, and it refutes the real polytheism, which is the Watch Tower's 'the Word was a god' (a second, lesser god). The Shema's word for 'one' (echad) is the same word used for a married couple becoming 'one flesh' and for 'one' cluster of many grapes — a oneness that can be composite. Hebrew had a word for a strictly solitary one (yachid) and the Shema does not use it. The point is not to prove the Trinity from one word, but to show that confessing one God does not require that God to be one person. Then turn it around: Jesus is given the one divine name, YHWH, and divine honour — so a faithful reading of the Shema must include him.

arguments.title: “Thee, the only true God” — John 17:3
arguments.shortClaim: The Witness argues that Jesus calls the Father 'the only true God' and distinguishes himself from him, so only the Father is God.

primaryReferences.text: Now this is eternal life: That they may know thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.
...that we may know the true God, and may be in his true Son. This is the true God and life eternal.

arguments.explanation: To call the Father 'the only true God' excludes false gods and idols; it does not exclude the Son, who shares the Father's one divine nature. Notice the sentence does not stop at the Father: eternal life is to know 'the only true God AND Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent' — the Son is placed alongside the Father as the joint object of the saving knowledge that is eternal life, which no mere creature could be. The incarnate Son, praying to the Father, naturally addresses him as God; that is the two-natures pattern again, not a denial of his own divinity. And John, who wrote this verse, also writes that Jesus is 'the true God and eternal life' (1 John 5:20) and that 'the Word was God' (John 1:1). The 'only true God' is one God — Father, Son, and Spirit — over against the idols the world worships.

arguments.title: “One mediator ... the man Christ Jesus” — 1 Timothy 2:5
arguments.shortClaim: The Witness argues that Paul calls Christ 'the man' and sets him between God and men, so Christ is not God but a human intermediary.

primaryReferences.text: For there is one God, and one mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus:

arguments.explanation: This verse states Christ's true humanity, which Catholics fully affirm — it does not deny his divinity. In fact it is a precise statement of why he can mediate: a mediator between God and men must touch both sides. Christ is the one mediator precisely because he is both God (able to reconcile) and man (able to represent us); 'the man Christ Jesus' names the humanity he took on in order to stand between. Calling him 'the man' no more denies his deity than calling him 'the Word' (John 1:1) denies his humanity — each title names one of his two natures. Far from reducing him to a creature, the verse presupposes that in the one person Christ Jesus, God and man meet.

arguments.title: “Before me there was no God formed” — Isaiah 43:10-11
arguments.shortClaim: The Witness argues that God says no god was formed before or after him and he is the only Saviour, so Jesus cannot be a (second) God or Saviour.

primaryReferences.text: You are my witnesses, saith the Lord, and my servant whom I have chosen: that you may know, and believe me, and understand that I myself am. Before me there was no God formed, and after me there shall be none.
I am, I am the Lord: and there is no saviour besides me.

arguments.explanation: This passage is the orthodox Christian's best friend, not the Witness's. God declares there is no other God and no other Saviour besides himself — so there is exactly one God and one Saviour. Now notice what the New Testament does with 'Saviour': it calls Jesus 'our Saviour' and even 'our great God and Saviour' (Titus 2:13; 2 Peter 1:1), and the angel says the newborn Jesus 'shall save his people from their sins' (Matthew 1:21). If God alone is Saviour (Isaiah 43:11) and Jesus is Saviour, then Jesus is included in the one God, not added as a rival. The verse rules out polytheism — which is exactly the problem with the Watch Tower's 'a god' Christ, a second lesser deity. Catholic doctrine has one God and one Saviour; the Witness position quietly has two.

arguments.title: “Ye are gods” — John 10:34-35 (Psalm 81:6 / 82:6)
arguments.shortClaim: The Witness argues that Jesus himself quotes 'you are gods' to show that being called 'god' does not mean being God — so calling Jesus 'god' need not mean he is God.

primaryReferences.text: Jesus answered them: Is it not written in your law: I said you are gods?

If he called them gods, to whom the word of God was spoken, and the scripture cannot be broken; Do you say of him whom the Father hath sanctified and sent into the world: Thou blasphemest, because I said, I am the Son of God?

primaryReferences.citation: Psalm 81:6 (= Psalm 82:6 in the Hebrew/modern numbering)
primaryReferences.text: I have said: You are gods and all of you the sons of the most High.

originalLanguage.note: Jesus cites Psalm 81:6 (82:6 in the Hebrew numbering), where God addresses the judges of Israel — men entrusted with his word and acting as his representatives — as 'gods' (elohim) and 'sons of the most High.' The title is applied to them by delegation, because the word of God came to them. Jesus' reasoning is a fortiori ('from the lesser to the greater'): if Scripture, which 'cannot be broken,' can call mere men 'gods' because God's word came to them, how much more may the one 'whom the Father hath sanctified and sent into the world' (v. 36) rightly call himself the Son of God? He is not lowering himself to their level — he is arguing that his claim is far more fitting than the honorific the Law already grants to lesser figures.

arguments.nwtRebuttal: The wording of John 10:34-35 is not itself disputed; the NWT reads similarly ('I said: “You are gods”?'). The dispute is over the INFERENCE the Watch Tower draws: that because the Law can call men 'gods,' calling Jesus 'god/a god' carries no claim to true deity. But that inverts Jesus' own argument: he reasons from the lesser (judges called 'gods' by delegation) to the greater (himself, sanctified and sent by the Father), so the passage strengthens, not weakens, his unique claim.
arguments.explanation: This is the one place a Witness can point to Jesus himself using 'gods' of mere men — so answer it on Jesus' own terms. In Psalm 81:6 (82:6 in the Hebrew numbering) God calls Israel's judges 'gods' and 'sons of the most High' because they were entrusted with his word and spoke in his name; the title is honorary and delegated. Jesus quotes this to the crowd that had just picked up stones because he, 'being a man,' made himself God (v. 33). His argument is from the lesser to the greater: if the inspired Scripture, which 'cannot be broken,' does not blaspheme by calling such men 'gods,' then it is no blasphemy for the one 'whom the Father hath sanctified and sent into the world' to call himself the Son of God (v. 36). Press the Witness on this: Jesus is NOT saying 'I'm a god in the same loose sense those judges were.' He is saying his claim is more justified than a title the Law already allows. And note what provoked the whole exchange — the crowd understood 'I and the Father are one' (v. 30) as a claim to deity, and Jesus answers by defending, not retracting, the claim. Rated 'strong' because the force rests on reading the a fortiori argument correctly, which the context (v. 30, v. 33, v. 36) makes plain.

arguments.title: “Nor the Son” — Mark 13:32 / Matthew 24:36
arguments.shortClaim: The Witness argues that if the Son does not know the day or hour, he cannot be the all-knowing God.

primaryReferences.text: But of that day or hour no man knoweth, neither the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but the Father.
...Lord, thou knowest all things: thou knowest that I love thee...

originalLanguage.text: οὐδὲ ὁ υἱός εἰ μὴ ὁ πατήρ
originalLanguage.translit: oude ho huios ei mē ho patēr
originalLanguage.note: The limitation is predicated of 'the Son' as incarnate. By the hypostatic union, Christ has two natures and so two kinds of knowledge: in his divine nature he knows all things (John 16:30; 21:17), while in his assumed human nature his knowledge, like his body, was truly human and could grow (Luke 2:52) and not possess, as something to communicate, the Father's timetable. The Douay-Rheims footnote on this verse says the Son 'knoweth it not, as our teacher; that is, he knoweth it not so as to teach it to us.'

arguments.explanation: Christ has two natures, divine and human, and this verse speaks of his human knowledge. As God, Jesus knows all things — his own disciples confess it: 'Lord, thou knowest all things' (John 21:17; 16:30). As man, his human mind was a real human mind that 'advanced in wisdom' (Luke 2:52); in that human capacity, the day of judgment was not his to announce. The ancient Catholic reading (noted even in the Douay-Rheims footnote) is that the Son does not know it 'as our teacher' — it was not given him to reveal. Two points for debate: first, the same logic that makes 'nor the Son' prove Jesus is not God would, in the same verse, prove the angels are not creatures of God's household — it proves too much. Second, a merely created being would hardly be ranked above all the angels and named second only to the Father in a statement about who knows the end.

arguments.title: “Why callest thou me good?” — Luke 18:19 / Mark 10:18
arguments.shortClaim: The Witness argues that Jesus denies being good like God ('none is good but God alone'), so he is distinguishing himself from God.

primaryReferences.text: And Jesus said to him: Why dost thou call me good? None is good but God alone.
And Jesus said to him: Why callest thou me good? None is good but one, that is God.

arguments.explanation: Jesus does not say 'I am not good' or 'I am not God.' He asks a question that invites the rich young ruler to think about what he just said. The ruler addressed Jesus as 'good master' as a mere flattering courtesy, treating him as one more respected teacher. Jesus' reply presses him: goodness in the full sense belongs to God alone — so if you rightly call me good, consider who you are really speaking to. It is a leading question, not a disclaimer. Far from denying divinity, the logic runs toward it: 'only God is good; you have called me good; think about that.' Elsewhere Jesus positively claims what belongs to God alone — to forgive sins, to receive worship, to be one with the Father — so this verse cannot be read as a confession that he is merely a man.

uncertainCitations.issue: DOUBLY contested, which is why this objection is rated 'supplementary.' (1) The Hebrew 'qanah' can mean 'possess/acquire/beget' (so DRA 'possessed me') or 'create'; the Septuagint read 'created' ('ektise'), which the Arians used. (2) Identifying the personified 'Wisdom' of this Hebrew poem with the pre-incarnate Son is an interpretive/devotional tradition, not a direct New Testament identification. Grant the ambiguity in debate and rely on clear NT texts instead.

Genuinely two-edged. 'archē' can mean 'beginning' (passive: first thing created, as the NWT takes it) or 'origin/source/ruler' (active: the orthodox reading, fitting Rev 1:17-18 and Col 1:16). The Greek permits both; context favours the active sense, but this verse alone will not settle the dispute. Rated 'strong,' not decisive.

TEXTUAL. The Challoner Douay-Rheims at Matthew 24:36 reads 'not the angels of heaven, but the Father alone' and OMITS 'nor the Son.' The 'nor the Son' clause is textually secure at the parallel Mark 13:32 (and is included in many Greek manuscripts of Matthew). Use Mark 13:32 as the primary citation for this objection; do not claim the DRA Matthew 24:36 contains the clause.

uncertainCitations.citation: John 14:28 ('the Father is greater than I')
uncertainCitations.issue: The verse is true on every reading; the only dispute is what 'greater' modifies (position/office of the incarnate Son vs inferiority of nature). The orthodox answer (greater in rank, equal in nature; cf. Phil 2:6-7) rests on the two-natures framework, which a Witness rejects at the outset — so this is answered as part of a systematic case, not as a single-verse knockout.

The 'compound unity' argument from 'echad' is contested by Hebraists: 'echad' most often simply means the numeral 'one.' Use it only to show the Shema does not EXCLUDE a plurality within the one God (it uses 'echad,' not the solitary 'yachid'), NOT to prove the Trinity from the word itself. The Shema's monotheism is affirmed by Catholics, not opposed by them.

Versification difference, labeled explicitly in the Colossians 1:15 argument: the verse cited as Psalm 89:27 in Hebrew/modern English Bibles is Psalm 88:28 in the Douay-Rheims (Vulgate numbering). Wording is unaffected; only the chapter/verse number differs.

TWO notes. (1) Versification: the psalm Jesus quotes ('I have said: You are gods') is Psalm 81:6 in the Douay-Rheims/Vulgate numbering but Psalm 82:6 in Hebrew/modern English Bibles; wording is unaffected, only the number differs. (2) The verse does not by itself PROVE Christ's divinity — it rebuts the Witness's inference. Its force depends on reading Jesus' argument as a fortiori (from the delegated 'gods' of the Law to the one 'sanctified and sent' by the Father), which the context (vv. 30, 33, 36) supports. Rated 'strong,' not decisive; it answers the objection rather than standing as an independent proof-text.
